title: Engineering Drawing OCR Pipeline
summary: From small, rotated labels in P&ID drawings to text that can be inspected and edited in a PDF workflow.
problem: Engineering drawings are not ordinary text documents. Small labels, rotated text, and complex geometry make extraction difficult; plain text output also loses the spatial context required for editing.
approach: I built a document-editing workflow around PaddleOCR and PaddleOCR-VL, with Python and FastAPI connecting extraction to application APIs. The workflow retains text and bounding boxes so extracted content can be reviewed and edited in context.
implementation: Used image preprocessing and OCR benchmarking to work on small and rotated labels.
Applied confidence analysis and bounding-box-based editing rather than treating extracted text as the final product.
Integrated the extraction workflow with backend application APIs using FastAPI.
challenges: Text correctness and geometric alignment are separate problems. An OCR output can read correctly but still be unusable for editing if its position or orientation is wrong.
tradeoffs: The engineering focus was inspectable output: preserve geometry and support review instead of presenting every OCR prediction as equally reliable. Comparative model benchmarks and coordinate round-trip errors are not published here.
outcome: Delivered an editable-document workflow around engineering drawings. A public accuracy benchmark, representative test set, and measured end-to-end latency have not been provided, so this case study does not claim numerical performance.

title: Self-RAG: Grounded Answers
summary: A LangGraph pipeline that decides when to retrieve, checks grounding, and bounds its revision and query-rewrite loops.
problem: Retrieving a document does not guarantee a supported or useful answer. A system also needs to decide whether retrieval is necessary and recognize when the source does not contain an answer.
approach: The public implementation uses structured LLM judgments to route retrieval, filter relevant chunks, check support, and assess usefulness. Unsupported answers are revised into direct quotes; unhelpful answers can trigger a rewritten retrieval query.
implementation: Uses typed Pydantic outputs for graph routing rather than parsing free-form model text.
Maintains separate retry budgets, documented as at most three answer revisions per retrieval and three retrieval-query rewrites.
Builds a per-session FAISS index for uploaded documents, with configurable model and embedding providers.
Includes offline graph tests with a scripted fake LLM so control-flow behavior can be tested without an API key.
challenges: A grounded answer can still be off-topic. Support checking and usefulness checking are separate gates, and missing-answer paths can consume more model calls than straightforward questions.
tradeoffs: The README explicitly documents the cost of repeated judging, less natural quote-only revisions, and the limitations of using the same model as writer and judge. Retry budgets prevent an unbounded loop; they do not guarantee answer correctness.
outcome: The repository documents working retrieval, direct-answer, revision, query-rewrite, and no-answer paths. These examples demonstrate control flow; no independently measured accuracy or production-scale latency result is claimed.
evidence: The public README, graph implementation, and offline tests support this case study. The repository does not currently provide a deployed-demo URL.

title: RAG Evaluation Framework
summary: An end-to-end PDF retrieval workflow with quality checks and structured experiment logs, beyond a plausible-looking answer.
problem: RAG quality depends on both the retrieved context and the generated answer. Looking at a few good examples does not reveal which stage is failing.
approach: I built a workflow for PDF ingestion, vector embeddings, semantic retrieval, and context-aware generation. DeepEval checks answer relevancy, faithfulness, contextual relevancy, and correctness; JSONL logs make runs and retrieval strategies comparable.
implementation: Connected document ingestion and semantic retrieval to a LangGraph generation workflow.
Separated context-oriented and answer-oriented evaluation criteria.
Recorded structured experiment outputs to compare strategies and inspect retrieval or generation bottlenecks.
challenges: A change can improve retrieval while leaving answer quality unchanged. Context relevance, answer support, and correctness need separate observations.
tradeoffs: Multiple quality dimensions provide a more useful picture than a single score, but evaluation thresholds, judge configuration, and test-set composition affect the interpretation. Those configuration details are not yet published here.
outcome: Built an automated evaluation and experiment-tracking workflow across four quality dimensions. No aggregate score or improvement percentage is shown because a reproducible benchmark has not been supplied.

title: Real-Time Speech Transcription
summary: Connecting live audio to multilingual speech recognition through Sarvam AI and LiveKit.
problem: Applications that process conversations need transcription while speech is arriving, including speech in multiple languages.
approach: At Flagestrator, I integrated Sarvam AI speech-to-text with the LiveKit SDK for real-time, multilingual transcription in enterprise AI applications.
implementation: Connected a real-time audio workflow to a speech-recognition integration.
Worked on multilingual transcription rather than an offline, single-language file demo.
challenges: Streaming integrations must bridge audio delivery and model output without making the application wait for a complete recording. Transport and recognition behavior need to be considered together.
tradeoffs: End-to-end latency and transcription quality should be measured separately. Buffering strategy, partial/final transcript handling, reconnection behavior, and language-level evaluation have not been supplied, so no specific design choice is asserted here.
outcome: Delivered a real-time multilingual transcription integration. No numerical latency, word-error rate, or concurrency benchmark is claimed.

title: LangGraph Research Assistant
summary: Parallel analyst interviews, web-grounded retrieval, and human approval inside a stateful research workflow.
problem: Research involves multiple perspectives, source gathering, repeated interviews, and synthesizing findings into a coherent report.
approach: I built an assistant that generates analyst personas, runs parallel interview workflows, and combines the research into Markdown reports. Tavily supports web-grounded retrieval, with human approval built into the graph.
implementation: Organized the workflow into reusable LangGraph nodes and shared state.
Used Pydantic models to structure data passed between workflow steps.
Kept human approval in the research flow rather than making all decisions autonomous.
challenges: Parallel work needs structured state and a synthesis step; simply running multiple prompts is not enough to produce a coherent report.
tradeoffs: Parallel interviews can explore multiple perspectives, while human approval adds a deliberate checkpoint. Runtime comparisons, source-quality evaluation, and failure-recovery behavior have not been published.
outcome: Built a stateful, human-in-the-loop research workflow that produces structured reports. No research-quality score or speedup is claimed.
